paras: The Texarkana barbecue killing was a fight at a barbecue at or near Texarkana on Thursday, August 12, 1880, in which one Black man was killed and two others were wounded. Known only from a brief Galveston News dispatch that was reprinted across the country as a one-line crime item, the report named none of those killed, wounded or involved.

According to a special to the Galveston News from Texarkana dated August 13, "In a row yesterday at a barbecue one negro was killed and two wounded." The Chicago Tribune's summary of the same news said that "the colored men" at the barbecue engaged in a "free flight" [fight], in which one man was killed and two others were severely injured. No report says how the man was killed, who killed him, or what began the quarrel.

No report of an arrest, inquest or prosecution appears in the coverage. The same Galveston dispatch went on to report a separate death: William Arnold, shot on the night of August 6, died declaring to the last that "Thad. Morris, a negro," had killed him. Arnold's race is not given, his shooting predated the barbecue by six days, and the Chicago Tribune printed it as a separate item headed "A Texas Murder" with no mention of the barbecue.

The story ran on August 13 and 14 in the Washington Evening Star, the Rock Island Argus, the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer, the Wheeling Register, the Chicago Tribune and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union. Weekly papers in Kansas, Ohio and Minnesota repeated it the following week in news digests. Headings placed it among routine crime news: the Evening Star used "Crime in Texas," the Wheeling Register "Trifles from Texas. The Usual List of Crimes from the Lone Star State," and the Topeka Tribune "A Texas Barbacue."
None of the white papers named the dead man, and no Black-press coverage of the killing was found.

The same-day dispatches all gave two wounded, while the Topeka Tribune's weekly digest a week later said five, a figure no other version repeats. Most versions placed Texarkana in Texas, but the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer wrote "Texarkana, Ark." In the separate Arnold report, the accused man appears as "Thad. Morris" in the Wheeling Register, "Thomas Norris" in the Lancaster paper, and "Norris" in the Topeka Tribune.

reader.title: Texarkana barbecue killing (1880)
bases: The reports describe a 'row' or 'free fight' among Black men at a barbecue in which one Black man was killed (A3, A5); none names a white participant or a racial motive.

Every version traces to one Galveston News special from Texarkana dated August 13 (A3, A4), condensed and reprinted elsewhere (A1, A2, A5, A7-A10); no local, follow-up or independent report was found.

accounts.label: Galveston News special from Texarkana
accounts.gist: In a row at a barbecue on August 12 one negro was killed and two wounded; the same dispatch separately reports William Arnold's death from a shooting on August 6.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune summary
accounts.gist: At a barbecue near Texarkana on Thursday 'the colored men' engaged in a free fight; one man was killed and two others severely injured.

accounts.label: Topeka Tribune weekly digest
accounts.gist: One negro killed and five wounded at the barbecue; Arnold died declaring Norris killed him.

framing.detail: Papers ran the dispatch as a one-sentence crime item with no names, under headings like 'Crime in Texas', 'Trifles from Texas: The Usual List of Crimes from the Lone Star State' and 'A Texas Barbacue'.

conflicts.note: The same-day dispatches all say two; five appears only in a weekly digest a week later and is likely a copying error.
Texarkana straddled the state line; the originating dispatch came through the Galveston News (A3, A4), and most versions say Texas.
Name of the man Arnold accused differs by version; this concerns the August 6 shooting, not the barbecue.

record_check.record: At a barbecue near Texarkana a Black man was killed; William Arnold, also shot, died saying Norris had killed him.
record_check.dossier: Arnold was shot on the night of August 6, six days before the barbecue, and no report links him to it; the barbecue was a fight among Black men in which one was killed and two wounded
Unnamed; per the Chicago Tribune, 'the colored men' at the barbecue fought among themselves
